1
  48
 
  The 
Monitor
 had been towed from New York and, despite a gale and stormy passage, had reached Hampton Roads on the Saturday evening at nine. Thence, in obedience to further orders, she proceeded two and a half hours later to a point alongside the 
Minnesota.
 At daylight on March 9, the Confederates saw a “craft such as the eyes of a seaman never looked upon before—an immense shingle floating on the water, with a gigantic cheese box rising from its centre: no sails, no wheels, no smoke-stack, no guns:”
 
2
 they knew it was the 
Monitor.
 At eight o’clock the 
Merrimac
 bore down upon the 
Minnesota
 and opened fire on her. The 
Monitor,
 which was commanded by Lieut. John L. Worden, steered directly for the 
Merrimac,
 “laid herself right alongside” and opened fire. The 
Monitor
 was of 776 tons burden, drew only ten and a half feet and had two 11-inch Dahlgren guns fired from a revolving turret; the 
Merrimac
 was a ship of 3500 tons carrying ten cannon. It was said that a pigmy strove against a giant; David had come out to encounter Goliath.
  49
 
  Then, for nearly four hours ensued a fierce artillery duel at close range; the distance between the two vessels varied from half a mile to a few yards. “Gun after gun was fired by the 
Monitor”
